topic: Bayes' Theorem and Independence: Unlocking Predictive Probability

outline.topic: Bayes' Theorem and Independence: Unlocking Predictive Probability

sections.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Concept of Conditional Probability
sections.content: Briefly define conditional probability P(A|B) using a Venn diagram. Visualize 'B' as the entire sample space, and 'A ∩ B' as the target portion within that space. This sets the stage for revising probabilities based on new evidence.
sections.example: Visualize a grid of 100 weather icons: 30 are 'Rain' and 70 are 'Sun'. If we know it is 'Cloudy', the 'Cloudy' subset becomes our new restricted universe.

sections.title: Independence: The 'No Influence' Rule
sections.content: Define independence: Events A and B are independent if P(A|B) = P(A). Explain this as a 'state of immunity' where knowing B provides zero information about A. Use a side-by-side animation: one set where circles change size (dependent) and one where they remain identical (independent).
sections.example: Flipping a coin (Independent: the second flip doesn't care about the first) vs. Drawing cards from a deck without replacement (Dependent: the odds change based on the previous draw).

sections.title: Introducing Bayes' Theorem: The Logic of Inference
sections.content: Introduce Bayes' Theorem: P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B). Use an animated flow chart showing the 'Prior' probability moving through a 'Likelihood' filter to reach the 'Posterior' (updated) probability.
sections.example: A smart robot detects a faulty sensor. 'Prior': The sensor is usually good. 'Likelihood': A faulty sensor produces this specific error code. 'Posterior': The updated probability that the robot is actually broken.

sections.title: Application and Wrap-up
sections.content: Synthesize the concepts. Show how we use Bayes' theorem to update our beliefs when new evidence emerges, contrasting this with independent events where evidence changes nothing. A final summary slide connects the formula back to the Venn diagram logic.
sections.example: A detective case: Given a piece of evidence (B), does it increase the probability of a suspect (A) being guilty? If the evidence is independent of the suspect, the probability remains unchanged, helping the detective rule out irrelevant clues.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Concept of Conditional Probability
lecture_lines: Conditional probability focuses on a restricted sample space.
Visualize all outcomes within the total set.
New evidence acts as a filtering constraint.
animations: Display Venn diagram showing overlapping sets A and B.
Highlight the intersection A ∩ B in color #FF5733.
Shrink the reference space to set B only.
Highlight the final ratio as P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B).

storyboard.title: Independence: The 'No Influence' Rule
lecture_lines: Independence means one event doesn't influence another.
Knowing event B provides zero information about A.
animations: Show two circles, A and B, widely separated.
Animate A moving without affecting B's position.
Display formula P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B) in color #33FF57.

storyboard.title: Introducing Bayes' Theorem: The Logic of Inference
lecture_lines: Bayes' Theorem updates beliefs with new evidence.
Starts with a prior belief about an event.
Multiplies by likelihood to get the posterior.
This process refines our understanding of probability.
It turns initial guesses into calculated conclusions.
animations: Fade in labels: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior.
Highlight P(A|B) and P(B|A) in contrasting colors #3357FF and #FF33A8.
Animate the transformation of prior to posterior.
Final emphasis on the complete equation logic.

storyboard.title: Application and Wrap-up
lecture_lines: Use Bayes' Theorem to refine predictions continuously.
Evidence shifts probability for dependent events.
Independent events ignore new, irrelevant information.
animations: Display a concrete medical test scenario.
Highlight the calculated probability result in color #FFFF33.
